items.title: Hecke row permutation modules and ordinary Dipper-James polytabloids
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ be the type-A Hecke algebra over $R$ with generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, quadratic relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant
commutation relations, and standard basis $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]],
[[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); here
$\ell(w)$ is the inversion length of $w\in S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). All modules below are right
modules.

**The star anti-involution.** Let $\sigma\mapsto\sigma^*$ be the unique
$R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$ for every generator: it
exists because reversal of words preserves the ideal of defining relations
(the quadratic and braid relators are fixed, while a distant commutation relator is sent to its negative), so reversal descends from the free algebra to $H$, and it is
unique because the generators generate $H$. On the standard basis
$T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$, since reversing a reduced word for $w$ is a reduced word
for $w^{-1}$.

**Tableau conventions.** Write $t\cdot\sigma$ for the right action of $S_n$ on
tableaux defined by $(t\cdot\sigma)(c):=\sigma^{-1}(t(c))$; it is the inverse
of the left action $(\sigma\cdot t)(c)=\sigma(t(c))$ of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]], and it is a right action.
A $\lambda$-tableau is **row standard** when its entries strictly increase
along every row; columns are not constrained. Let $t^\lambda$ be the row-filled
$\lambda$-tableau, whose row $i$ carries
$\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\dots,\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i$ from left
to right, and let $t_\lambda$ be the column-filled $\lambda$-tableau, whose
column $j$ carries consecutive integers downward; equivalently
$t_\lambda(i,j)=t^{\lambda'}(j,i)$, so that $t_\lambda$ is the transpose of
$t^{\lambda'}$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

**The row subgroup and the coset representatives.** Let $S_\lambda$ be the
**row subgroup** of $\lambda$, the subgroup of $S_n$ preserving every row of
$t^\lambda$; writing
$$B_i:=\{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+1,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_{i-1}+2,\ \dots,\ \lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_i\}$$
for the $i$-th row block of $t^\lambda$, one has
$S_\lambda=S(B_1)\times\cdots\times S(B_k)$, the direct product of the
symmetric groups of the individual row blocks. Let
$$D_\lambda:=\{d\in S_n:t^\lambda\cdot d\text{ is row standard}\}.$$
This is the set of minimal-length right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in
$S_n$: every right coset $S_\lambda d$ has exactly one element $d_0$ for which
$t^\lambda\cdot d_0$ is row standard, and it satisfies
$\ell(wd_0)=\ell(w)+\ell(d_0)$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). Let
$w_\lambda\in S_n$ be the unique element with $t^\lambda\cdot w_\lambda=t_\lambda$;
existence and uniqueness hold because the action of $S_n$ on $\lambda$-tableaux
is free and transitive.

**Generators and modules.** For a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w,\qquad y_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}T_w,\qquad z_\lambda:=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_{\lambda'},$$
where $\lambda'$ is the conjugate partition of $\lambda$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). The **row
permutation module** is the right ideal $M(\lambda):=x_\lambda H\subseteq H$,
and the **ordinary Dipper-James polytabloid module** is
$P(\lambda):=z_\lambda H\subseteq M(\lambda)$; $z_\lambda$ is its polytabloid
generator.

**The forms.** The **permutation form** is the $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ determined on the distinguished family
$\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ by
$$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}\qquad(d,e\in D_\lambda),$$
and the **DJ form** is the restriction of $\beta$ to $P(\lambda)$. That family
is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$
([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]), so the displayed
values define a unique bilinear form; the family is $\{x_\varnothing\}=\{1\}$
for the empty partition.

**Small cases and base change.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ set
$x_\varnothing=y_\varnothing=z_\varnothing=1$, so that
$M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ and $\beta$ is the standard form; for
$n=0,1$ there are no generators and $H=R$. Every base change
$A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, produces all
objects above over $R$ by the same formulas; the suppliers of this page prove
that the distinguished families and the form are compatible with such base
change. No choice principle is used.

## Remarks

- **Normalization dictionary.** Fayers' Section 2.1 list of notation is the
  source of the displayed formulas, in the normalization
  $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$ used here. Heard-Kujawa use the symmetric normalization
  $(T_i-q)(T_i+q^{-1})=0$ with $x_\lambda=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}q^{\ell(w)}T_w$;
  their generator $z_\lambda=x_\lambda T_{\sigma_\lambda}y_{\lambda^{\mathsf T}}$
  and their standard-basis indexing by standard tableaux of the transposed
  shape match the construction here, but the exact coefficients differ and only
  the combinatorial shape of the construction is taken from that source.
  Mathas' Chapter 3 uses the same normalization as this item.

- **Orientation of the dictionaries.** Fayers lets functions act on the
  right. Interpreting the source's label $j\sigma$ as $\sigma^{-1}(j)$ in
  the library's function-composition convention gives exactly the right
  tableau action used here. Reduced words in the adjacent transpositions
  then identify the algebra presentations and their coset and tableau indices.

- **Definitional scope of the form.** The permutation form is fixed here by its
  values on the distinguished basis and is a chosen contravariant form; its
  restriction to $P(\lambda)$ is taken as the definition of the DJ form. The
  historical Dipper-James self-form on $S^\lambda$ is this restriction, not an
  additional source claim, and nondegeneracy of $\beta$ or of its restriction
  is not asserted here.

- **The empty and rank-zero cases.** For $\lambda=\varnothing$ the row group is
  $S_\varnothing=S_0=\{1\}$, the group $D_\varnothing=\{1\}$ is a singleton, and
  $M(\varnothing)=P(\varnothing)=R$ with basis $\{T_{\mathrm{id}}\}=\{1\}$, indexed by the identity of $S_0$.

items.title: The row permutation module: distinguished basis and Hecke action
items.statement:
In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and every $q\in R^\times$:

1. $M(\lambda)$ is free with basis $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$;

2. $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$
for every $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$;

3. if $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$ and $s=t\cdot s_i=t^\lambda\cdot d'$, then
$$x_\lambda T_dT_i=\begin{cases}q\,x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is not row standard},\\ x_\lambda T_{d'},&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')>\ell(d),\\ q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}+(q-1)x_\lambda T_d,&s\text{ is row standard and }\ell(d')<\ell(d);\end{cases}$$

4. the basis and the action formulas are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$ along a ring map sending $q$ to a unit.

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Length and multiplication criteria for one generator.** Let $g\in S_n$ and $1\le i<n$. The one-line list of $gs_i$ is obtained from that of $g$ by exchanging the entries $g(i),g(i+1)$ at positions $i,i+1$, and only the relative order of this single pair changes, so $\ell(gs_i)=\ell(g)+1$ if $g(i)<g(i+1)$ and $\ell(gs_i)=\ell(g)-1$ if $g(i)>g(i+1)$. Replacing $g$ by $g^{-1}$ gives $\ell(s_ig)=\ell(g^{-1}s_i)$ equal to $\ell(g)+1$ if and only if $g^{-1}(i)<g^{-1}(i+1)$; under this hypothesis the multiplication rule gives $T_gT_i=T_{gs_i}$, and applying the same rule to $g^{-1}$ and then $*$ gives $T_{s_i}T_g=T_{s_ig}$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 **Order preservation inside rows.** If $d\in D_\lambda$ and $a<b$ are entries lying in the same row of $t^\lambda$, then $d^{-1}(a)<d^{-1}(b)$. Indeed the boxes of $a$ and $b$ lie in that row with the box of $a$ to the left, and $t^\lambda\cdot d=d^{-1}\cdot t^\lambda$ carries those boxes to the entries $d^{-1}(a),d^{-1}(b)$; since $t^\lambda\cdot d$ is row standard, its entries increase along the row. [F4, algebra]

1.3 **The coset representatives.** The row sets of $t^\lambda\cdot g$ are $g^{-1}(B_1),\dots,g^{-1}(B_k)$ by [F4], so $t^\lambda\cdot g$ and $t^\lambda\cdot g'$ have the same row sets if and only if $g'g^{-1}$ preserves every $B_r$, that is, if and only if $g'\in S_\lambda g$. For a given right coset $S_\lambda g$, the tableau $t^\lambda\cdot g$ has some row sets; filling each row by its entries in increasing order gives a row-standard tableau with the same row sets, and it equals $t^\lambda\cdot y$ for some $y\in S_n$ because the action of $S_n$ on tableaux is transitive. That $y$ lies in $S_\lambda g$, since it has the same row sets as $t^\lambda\cdot g$. Two row-standard tableaux with the same row sets are equal, and the action on tableaux is free, so $y$ is unique in its coset; hence $D_\lambda$ is a complete set of right coset representatives of $S_\lambda$ in $S_n$. [F4, algebra]

1.4 **The parabolic identities.** For every $w\in S_\lambda$ one has $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$, $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$. For a generator $s_i\in S_\lambda$ split $S_\lambda$ into $A=\{u:\ell(us_i)>\ell(u)\}$ and its complement $B$; right multiplication by $s_i$ bijects $A$ onto $B$, and the multiplication rule gives $$x_\lambda T_i=\sum_{u\in A}T_{us_i}+\sum_{u\in B}\bigl((q-1)T_u+qT_{us_i}\bigr)=\sum_{v\in B}T_v+(q-1)\sum_{u\in B}T_u+q\sum_{v\in A}T_v=q\,x_\lambda.$$ Since every product $us_i$ with $u\in S_\lambda$ lies in $S_\lambda$, induction on $\ell(w)=\ell(vs_i)=\ell(v)+1$ gives $x_\lambda T_w=(x_\lambda T_v)T_i=q^{\ell(v)}q\,x_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$. The star map sends each $T_w$ to $T_{w^{-1}}$ and permutes the sum $x_\lambda$, so $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$; then $(T_wx_\lambda)^*=x_\lambda T_{w^{-1}}=q^{\ell(w^{-1})}x_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ by [F2], and applying $*$ again gives $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 **Length additivity and multiplicativity.** For $w\in S_\lambda$ and $d\in D_\lambda$ one has $\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$ and $T_wT_d=T_{wd}$. Prove this by induction on $\ell(w)$. For $w=1$ both claims are immediate. For $\ell(w)\ge1$ write $w=s_iv$ with $s_i\in S_\lambda$ a simple reflection of $S_\lambda$ and $\ell(w)=1+\ell(v)$; then $\ell(s_iv)=\ell(v)+1$, so $v^{-1}(i)<v^{-1}(i+1)$ by step 1.1. Because $s_i\in S_\lambda$, the labels $i,i+1$ lie in one row block $B_r$, and $v^{-1}\in S_\lambda$ preserves every row block, so $v^{-1}(i)$ and $v^{-1}(i+1)$ lie in the same row of $t^\lambda$; step 1.2 then gives $(vd)^{-1}(i)=d^{-1}(v^{-1}(i))<d^{-1}(v^{-1}(i+1))=(vd)^{-1}(i+1)$, whence $\ell(s_ivd)=\ell(vd)+1$ by step 1.1. The induction hypothesis gives $\ell(vd)=\ell(v)+\ell(d)$, so $\ell(wd)=\ell(s_ivd)=\ell(v)+1+\ell(d)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$. For the basis elements, step 1.1 gives $T_{s_i}T_{vd}=T_{s_ivd}$ since $\ell(s_ivd)=\ell(vd)+1$, so $T_wT_d=T_{s_i}(T_vT_d)=T_{s_i}T_{vd}=T_{wd}$ using the induction hypothesis $T_vT_d=T_{vd}$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, algebra]

2.2 **The shape of the three cases.** Let $d\in D_\lambda$, $t=t^\lambda\cdot d$, $s=t\cdot s_i=s_i\cdot t=t^\lambda\cdot(ds_i)$. First, $s$ is row standard if and only if $i$ and $i+1$ lie in different rows of $t$: if they lie in the same row then $i$ is left of $i+1$ and the swap creates a descent in that row, while if they lie in different rows then each affected row keeps the same two neighbours of the moved entry, the left neighbour smaller than $i$ and the right neighbour larger than $i+1$, so both inequalities persist. Second, the position of a label $j$ in the row-reading word of $t$ equals $d(j)$, because $t=d^{-1}\cdot t^\lambda$; so by step 1.1, $\ell(ds_i)=\ell(d)+1$ holds exactly when $i$ precedes $i+1$ in $t$, and this happens in particular when $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row. [step 1.1, F4, algebra]

3.1 **The basis.** For $d\in D_\lambda$, step 2.1 gives $x_\lambda T_d=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_wT_d=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_{wd}$, whose support in the standard basis is exactly the right coset $S_\lambda d$ with coefficient $1$ at every element. By step 1.3 the cosets $S_\lambda d$, $d\in D_\lambda$, are pairwise disjoint and partition $S_n$, so the supports of the $x_\lambda T_d$ are disjoint; since the $T_w$ are $R$-linearly independent by [F1], the family $\{x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ is linearly independent. For an arbitrary $g\in S_n$, step 1.3 lets us write $g=wd$ with $w\in S_\lambda$, $d\in D_\lambda$, and then $x_\lambda T_g=x_\lambda T_wT_d=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda T_d$ by steps 2.1 and 1.4; since the $T_g$ span $H$ by [F1], the family spans the right ideal $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H$. Hence it is a basis and $M(\lambda)$ is free, which is clause (1). [step 1.3, step 1.4, step 2.1, F1]

3.2 **Case of one row.** Suppose $i$ and $i+1$ lie in the same row of $t$. Then $s$ has the same row sets as $t$, so $ds_i$ and $d$ lie in the same right coset of $S_\lambda$ by step 1.3, say $ds_i=wd$ with $w\in S_\lambda$. By steps 2.1 and 2.2, $\ell(d)+1=\ell(ds_i)=\ell(wd)=\ell(w)+\ell(d)$, so $\ell(w)=1$. The multiplication rule [F1] and step 2.2 give $x_\lambda T_dT_i=x_\lambda T_{ds_i}=x_\lambda T_{wd}=x_\lambda T_wT_d=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda T_d=q\,x_\lambda T_d$, using step 1.4. This is the first displayed case. [F1, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 **Case of two rows.** Suppose $i$ and $i+1$ lie in different rows of $t$. Then $s$ is row standard by step 2.2, so $d':=ds_i$ lies in $D_\lambda$ and $t^\lambda\cdot d'=s$; this is the element $d'$ of the statement. The multiplication rule [F1] gives $x_\lambda T_dT_i=x_\lambda T_{d'}$ if $\ell(d')=\ell(d)+1$, and $x_\lambda T_dT_i=(q-1)x_\lambda T_d+q\,x_\lambda T_{d'}$ if $\ell(d')=\ell(d)-1$. These are the second and third displayed cases, and together with step 3.2 they prove clause (3). [F1, step 2.2, step 3.2]

4.2 **Base change.** All constructions above are defined over an arbitrary commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$ by the formulas of [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], and every identity was obtained from the presentation and from inversion counts, so its coefficients are Laurent polynomials in $q$ with integer coefficients. Given a ring map $R\to R'$ with $q\mapsto q'\in(R')^\times$, the base change sends $H_{R,q}(S_n)$ to $H_{R',q'}(S_n)$ and the elements $T_w$, $x_\lambda$ to their images $T'_w$, $x'_\lambda$; the basis $\{x_\lambda T_d\}$ maps to the corresponding basis, and the formulas of steps 1.4, 2.1 and 3.1 specialize termwise, so clause (4) follows. [step 1.4, step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, algebra]

5.1 Clauses (1), (2), (3) and (4) are established by steps 3.1, 1.4, 3.2, 4.1 and 4.2. Only inversion counts, the presentation of $H$, the structure of the row groups and the standard basis are used; no choice principle is used. [step 1.4, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

items.title: The permutation form is H-contravariant and restricts to the DJ form
items.statement:
In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$, the permutation form $\beta$ on

## Statement

In the notation of
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], for every
commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$, the permutation form $\beta$ on
$M(\lambda)$ is well defined, symmetric and $R$-bilinear, with
$\beta(x_\lambda T_d,x_\lambda T_e)=\delta_{d,e}q^{\ell(d)}$ on the
distinguished basis of
[[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]. It is
$H$-contravariant:
$$\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)\qquad(x,y\in M(\lambda),\ h\in H).$$
Its restriction $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ to the polytabloid module $P(\lambda)$
satisfies the same identity for $x,y\in P(\lambda)$ and is called the DJ form.
Both $\beta$ and $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ are compatible with every base change
$R\to R'$. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^\times$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with the standard basis $\{T_w\}$, and the modules $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H\supseteq P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with the distinguished basis $\{x_d:=x_\lambda T_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ of [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]].

[F1] $\{x_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$, and for each generator $T_i$ the action on it is: $x_dT_i=qx_d$ when $i,i+1$ lie in the same row of the tableau $t^\lambda\cdot d$; otherwise $d^*:=ds_i\in D_\lambda$ and $x_dT_i=x_{d^*}$ if $\ell(d^*)>\ell(d)$, while $x_dT_i=qx_{d^*}+(q-1)x_d$ if $\ell(d^*)<\ell(d)$. Moreover $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ is a right ideal of $H$ contained in $M(\lambda)$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]).

[F2] The star map is an $R$-algebra anti-automorphism of $H$ with $T_i^*=T_i$; in particular it sends a product of generators to the reversed product ([[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]).

[F3] $H$ is generated as an $R$-algebra by $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, and all modules are right modules ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The form is well defined, symmetric and bilinear.** By [F1] the family $\{x_d:d\in D_\lambda\}$ is an $R$-basis of $M(\lambda)$, so there is exactly one $R$-bilinear form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ whose Gram matrix in this basis is the diagonal matrix with entries $q^{\ell(d)}$, $d\in D_\lambda$; this form is symmetric because its Gram matrix is diagonal, and it is the permutation form of the statement. For $\lambda=\varnothing$ the basis is $\{1\}$ and $\beta(1,1)=q^0=1$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 **Orbits of one generator.** Fix $i$ and abbreviate $x_d:=x_\lambda T_d$. Partition $D_\lambda$ into the set $S$ of those $d$ for which $i,i+1$ lie in the same row of $t^\lambda\cdot d$, and the remaining set $D$; for $d\in D$ the element $d^*:=ds_i$ again lies in $D_\lambda$ and $(d^*)^*=d$, by the second and third cases of [F1] applied twice. Thus $D$ is partitioned into two-element orbits $\{u,v\}$ with $v=us_i$ and $\ell(v)=\ell(u)+1$, and the action on such an orbit is $x_uT_i=x_v$, $x_vT_i=qx_u+(q-1)x_v$, while $x_dT_i=qx_d$ for $d\in S$. In particular each $x_dT_i$ lies in the span of the orbit of $d$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 **Self-adjointness of the generators.** In an orbit $\{u,v\}$ with $\ell(v)=\ell(u)+1$, the two diagonal pairings are $\beta(x_uT_i,x_u)=\beta(x_u,x_uT_i)=0$ and $\beta(x_vT_i,x_v)=\beta(x_v,x_vT_i)=(q-1)q^{\ell(v)}$. The two off-diagonal pairings both equal $q^{\ell(v)}=q\,q^{\ell(u)}$ by the action in step 1.2. A singleton orbit contributes $q\,q^{\ell(d)}$ on its diagonal, and pairings between distinct orbit spans vanish. Thus $\beta(xT_i,y)=\beta(x,yT_i)$ on basis vectors and hence, by bilinearity, on all of $M(\lambda)$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, algebra]

3.1 **Words, all of $H$, and restriction.** For every word $h=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_r}$ of generators and all $x,y\in M(\lambda)$ one has $\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)$, where $h^*=T_{i_r}\cdots T_{i_1}$: this follows from step 2.1 by induction on $r$, moving one generator at a time from the first to the second argument. Since the generators span $H$ as an $R$-algebra by [F3], every $h\in H$ is a finite $R$-linear combination of such words, and by [F2] the element $h^*$ is obtained from the same expression by reversing each word; bilinearity therefore gives $\beta(xh,y)=\beta(x,yh^*)$ for all $h\in H$. Finally $P(\lambda)$ is a right ideal contained in $M(\lambda)$ by [F1], so the same identity holds for $x,y\in P(\lambda)$; its restriction to $P(\lambda)$ is the DJ form of the statement. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 **Base change.** Under a ring map $R\to R'$ with $q\mapsto q'\in(R')^\times$, the distinguished basis identifies $R'\otimes_RM(\lambda)$ with $M_{R'}(\lambda)$ and the diagonal weights specialize, identifying the scalar extension of $\beta$ with $\beta'$. The natural map $j:R'\otimes_RP(\lambda)\to M_{R'}(\lambda)$ has image $P_{R'}(\lambda)$: the vectors $z_\lambda T_w$ span $P(\lambda)$ and their images $z'_\lambda T'_w$ span $P_{R'}(\lambda)$. For pure tensors, and then by bilinearity, $\beta'(j(a\otimes p),j(b\otimes r))=ab\,\beta(p,r)$. This proves compatibility of the restricted forms along the natural map, without inferring injectivity of a tensor map from right exactness; the later split polytabloid basis establishes that this map is also an isomorphism. Contravariance specializes by the same identity. [step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra]

5.1 The permutation form is well defined, symmetric and bilinear by step 1.1, is $H$-contravariant by step 3.1, and its restriction to $P(\lambda)$ satisfies the same identity; both forms are base-change compatible by step 4.1. Only the distinguished basis, inversion counts and the algebra structure of $H$ are used; no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

items.title: The Hecke sign automorphism, pullback and contragredient dual
items.statement:
For every commutative ring $R$ and $q\in R^\times$:

1. $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i=-qT_i^{-1}$ extends uniquely to an involutive
$R$-algebra automorphism $\theta$ of $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, with
$\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$; $\theta$ commutes with the star
anti-involution $*$ and is compatible with every base change.

2. For a right $H$-module $M$, the pullback $M^\theta$ (same underlying
$R$-module, action $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$) is a right $H$-module; $(-)^\theta$
is exact, preserves submodules, quotients, finite composition multiplicities and
simplicity, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$.

3. The star-contragredient $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with
$(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$ is a right $H$-module; for finite free $M$ it is finite
free of the same rank, $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change, and
$(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$.

4. For every partition $\lambda\vdash n$, if $w_0(S_\lambda)$ is the longest
element of the row subgroup, then
$$\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda,\qquad \theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}x_\lambda.$$
In particular $\theta(x_\lambda)$ and $y_\lambda$ differ by the unit
$q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$, and this unit factor must be carried through every
form comparison. At $q=1$, $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism
$w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$ of $R[S_n]$.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^\times$, $n\ge0$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with generators $T_i$, standard basis $\{T_w\}$ and star anti-involution $*$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with row subgroup $S_\lambda$ and its longest element $w_0(S_\lambda)$ (of length $N:=\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))$), and the elements $x_\lambda,y_\lambda$ of [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]].

[F1] In $H$ the relations $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations hold, $\{T_w\}$ is an $R$-basis, $T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}$ if $\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1$ and $T_wT_i=(q-1)T_w+qT_{ws_i}$ if $\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1$; the same rule holds on the left, $T_iT_w=T_{s_iw}$ respectively $T_iT_w=(q-1)T_w+qT_{s_iw}$. Moreover $T_i^{-1}=q^{-1}(T_i-(q-1))$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).

[F2] $*$ is an $R$-algebra anti-automorphism with $T_i^*=T_i$ and $T_w^*=T_{w^{-1}}$; the generators $T_i$ generate $H$ as an $R$-algebra ([[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]).

[F3] $x_\lambda T_w=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ and $T_wx_\lambda=q^{\ell(w)}x_\lambda$ for $w\in S_\lambda$, and $x_\lambda^*=x_\lambda$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]).

[F4] For a commutative ring $R$ and $n\in\mathbb N$ the map $\operatorname{Hom}_R(R^n,N)\to N^n$, $f\mapsto(f(e_1),\dots,f(e_n))$, is an isomorphism of $R$-modules ([[lem-hom-from-a-finite-free-module]]).

[F5] The specialization construction: $H_{R,q}(S_n)$ is the base change $R\otimes_AH_v(n)$ along $v\mapsto q$, and all formulas with coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ specialize ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The automorphism and its first properties.** Put $\theta(T_i):=(q-1)-T_i$. Since $T_i^{-1}=q^{-1}(T_i-(q-1))$ by [F1], one has $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$. The assignment satisfies the Hecke relations: $\theta(T_i)^2=(q-1)^2-2(q-1)T_i+T_i^2=(q-1)^2-2(q-1)T_i+(q-1)T_i+q=(q-1)\theta(T_i)+q$; the braid relation holds because $\theta(T_i)=-qT_i^{-1}$ multiplies every generator by the same scalar $-q$, and inverses satisfy the braid relations; the distant commutation holds similarly, and the scalar squares cancel. Since $H$ is presented by these relations, the assignment extends uniquely to an $R$-algebra endomorphism $\theta$ of $H$; applying it twice fixes each generator, so $\theta^2=\mathrm{id}_H$ by [F2] and $\theta$ is an involutive automorphism. For a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$ one gets $\theta(T_w)=(-q)^\ell T_{i_1}^{-1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}^{-1}=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$, and $\theta$ commutes with $*$ because both sides of $\theta(T_w^*)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_w^{-1}$ and $\theta(T_w)^*=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-*}=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_w^{-1}$ agree. All generator images have coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, so $\theta$ is compatible with base change by [F5]. [F1, F2, F5, algebra]

1.2 **Pullback of modules.** If $M$ is a right $H$-module, then $M^\theta$ with $m\cdot h:=m\theta(h)$ is a right $H$-module, because $(m\cdot h)\cdot k=m\theta(h)\theta(k)=m\theta(hk)=m\cdot(hk)$. Since $\theta$ is an involutive automorphism, the assignments $M\mapsto M^\theta$ on modules and $N\mapsto N$ on underlying $R$-modules are inverse bijections on submodules: a subset $N\subseteq M$ is closed under the old action if and only if it is closed under the new one, since $\theta$ is bijective and $\theta(H)=H$. Hence $(-)^\theta$ is exact, preserves submodules and quotients, and $(M^\theta)^\theta=M$; it also carries simple modules to simple modules and preserves the length of finite composition series with multiplicities, because the two module structures have exactly the same submodule lattice. [F2, algebra]

2.1 **Contragredient modules.** For a right $H$-module $M$, put $M^\circ:=\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$ with $(f\cdot h)(m):=f(mh^*)$. Then $((f\cdot h)\cdot k)(m)=f(mk^*h^*)=f(m(hk)^*)$ by [F2], so $f\cdot(hk)=(f\cdot h)\cdot k$ and $M^\circ$ is a right $H$-module. If $M\cong R^r$ is finite free, then $M^\circ\cong R^r$ by [F4] applied with $N=R$, and the dual-basis identification is natural in $R$, so $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change. Finally $(M^\theta)^\circ=(M^\circ)^\theta$: both have underlying module $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R)$, and for the two actions one computes $(f\cdot h)(m)=f(m\theta(h^*))$ for the first and $(f\cdot h)(m)=f(m\theta(h)^*)=f(m\theta(h^*))$ for the second, using that $\theta$ commutes with $*$ by step 1.1. [step 1.1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.2 **The common eigenspace.** Let $H_\lambda$ be the $R$-span of $\{T_w:w\in S_\lambda\}$, the subalgebra generated by the $T_i$ with $s_i\in S_\lambda$; it is $\theta$-stable because $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i\in H_\lambda$. The element $\theta(x_\lambda)$ lies in $H_\lambda$ and satisfies $T_i\theta(x_\lambda)=\theta(\theta(T_i)x_\lambda)=\theta(((q-1)-T_i)x_\lambda)=\theta((q-1)x_\lambda-qx_\lambda)=-\theta(x_\lambda)$ for every generator $T_i$ of $S_\lambda$, by [F3]; so it is a common left eigenvector for eigenvalue $-1$. Conversely let $a=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}a_wT_w\in H_\lambda$ satisfy $T_ia=-a$ for all these generators. Comparing in the expansion $T_ia=\sum_wa_wT_iT_w$, using the left multiplication rule of [F1], the coefficient of $T_v$ equals $qa_{s_iv}$ when $\ell(s_iv)=\ell(v)+1$ and equals $(q-1)a_v+a_{s_iv}$ when $\ell(s_iv)=\ell(v)-1$, and it must equal $-a_v$; the first case gives $a_{s_iv}=-q^{-1}a_v$, and the second gives the same relation with the roles of $v$ and $s_iv$ exchanged. Hence $a_{s_iu}=-q^{-1}a_u$ whenever $\ell(s_iu)=\ell(u)+1$. Every nonidentity $w\in S_\lambda$ is a length-increasing product of generators of $S_\lambda$: the permutation $w^{-1}$ restricted to some row block $B_r$ is not the identity, hence has an adjacent descent, which exhibits a generator $s_i$ of $S_\lambda$ with $\ell(s_iw)=\ell(w)-1$. Iterating, $a_w=(-q)^{-\ell(w)}a_1$ for all $w\in S_\lambda$, so $a=a_1y_\lambda$: the common eigenspace is exactly the free line $Ry_\lambda$, and it contains $\theta(x_\lambda)$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra]

2.3 **The case $q=1$.** At $q=1$ the quadratic relation is $T_i^2=1$, so $T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}=T_w$ and step 1.1 gives $\theta(T_w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}T_w=\operatorname{sgn}(w)T_w$. The relations $T_i^2=1$, braid and distant commutation are the Coxeter relations of the adjacent transpositions of $S_n$, so the specialization $H_{R,1}(S_n)$ is the group algebra $R[S_n]$ with $T_w$ the group basis element $w$; the displayed identity then says that $\theta$ is the pullback along the sign automorphism $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$. For $N=0$, as in the shapes $\varnothing$ and $(1^n)$, the unit below is $q^0=1$. [step 1.1, F5, algebra]

3.1 **The unit.** By step 2.2 write $\theta(x_\lambda)=c\,y_\lambda$ with $c\in R$. In the expansion $\theta(T_w)=\prod_j\theta(T_{i_j})=\prod_j((q-1)-T_{i_j})$ of a reduced word, every term other than the full product of the $-T_{i_j}$ has fewer than $\ell(w)$ generator factors and so cannot contribute to the standard basis element of length $N$; hence the coefficient of $T_{w_0(S_\lambda)}$ in $\theta(x_\lambda)=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}\theta(T_w)$ is $(-1)^N$, the contribution of $w=w_0(S_\lambda)$ alone. In $c\,y_\lambda$ the coefficient of $T_{w_0(S_\lambda)}$ is $c(-q)^{-N}$, so $c=(-1)^N(-q)^N=q^N$. Therefore $\theta(x_\lambda)=q^Ny_\lambda$, and applying the involution $\theta$ and using $\theta(q^N)=q^N$ gives $\theta(y_\lambda)=q^{-N}x_\lambda$. [step 2.2, step 1.1, F1, algebra]

4.1 Statements (1), (2), (3) and (4) are established by steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1, with the $q=1$ clause in step 2.3 and the unit $q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}$ displayed in step 3.1. Only the presentation of $H$, inversion counts, the standard basis and finite free duality are used; no choice principle is used. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.3, step 3.1] ∎

items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $n\ge0$, and let
$\alpha,\nu\vdash n$ be partitions of $n$ with conjugate $\nu'$ and
$x_\alpha,y_\nu\in H_{R,q}(S_n)$ as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. If $\alpha$
is not dominated by $\nu'$ in the sense of
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], that is, if
$\sum_{i\le k}\alpha_i>\sum_{i\le k}\nu'_i$ for some $k\ge1$, then
$$x_\alpha Hy_\nu=0.$$
The vanishing is a universal Laurent-polynomial identity, remains valid at
singular parameters and uses no cancellation of $q+1$. The proof explicitly
sorts parabolic double cosets and uses the zero product
$(1+T_i)(1-q^{-1}T_i)=0$. Empty shapes and $n=0,1$ are included. No choice
principle is used.

items.title: The Murphy cellular basis, the cell law and the Murphy form
items.statement:
For every commutative ring $R$, every $q\in R^\times$, and every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ with row symmetrizer $m_\lambda=x_\lambda$, put
$m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^*m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$ for standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$,
where $d(t)\in D_\lambda$ is the element with $t^\lambda\cdot d(t)=t$. Then:

1. $\{m_{st}:\lambda\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ is an
$R$-basis of $H$ (the **Murphy basis**), and $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$.

2. The $R$-spans $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\unrhd\lambda\}$ and
$I^{\rhd\lambda}$ of $\{m_{uv}:\mu\rhd\lambda\}$ are two-sided ideals of $H$
(dominance order), and $I^{\unrhd\lambda}/I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is free with basis
the classes of $\{m_{st}:s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$.

3. The **Murphy cell module**
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ is free
with basis $\{m_t:=x_\lambda T_{d(t)}+I^{\rhd\lambda}:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$
and satisfies the **cell law**: for $h\in H$ and standard $s,t$,
$$m_{st}h\equiv\sum_{v\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)}r_v\,m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}},\qquad r_v\in R,$$
with coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$.

4. There is a unique $R$-bilinear **Murphy form** $G_\lambda$ on
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with
$m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\lambda}}$; it is
symmetric, associative in the sense
$G_\lambda(m_sh,m_t)=G_\lambda(m_s,m_th^*)$, and its radical is a submodule of
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$.

5. The basis, the ideals, the cell law and the form are compatible with every
base change.

The proof also supplies the auxiliary identities used by the comparison:
$\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$ defines a trace with
$\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ (step 1.3); for a composition
$\alpha$ and the partition $\beta$ obtained by sorting its parts,
$x_\alpha=T_dx_\beta T_d^{-1}$ with a block-reordering permutation $d$
(step 2.2); and for the Garnir composition $\alpha$ at a node of $\rho$,
$x_\rho\sum_{d\in S_\alpha\cap D_\rho}T_d
=\sum_{v\in S_\rho\cap D_\alpha}T_v^*x_\alpha$ (step 2.3).
The block-reordering and Garnir data are specified in those steps.

In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is finite free of rank
$f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$. No choice principle is used.

items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $q\in R^\times$, let $\lambda\vdash n$
with conjugate $\mu=\lambda'$, and let $H$, $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H$,
$P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with $z_\lambda=x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}y_\mu$, the
permutation form $\beta$ and the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ be as in
[[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]]. Write
$b_r:=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}$ for the row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $r$
(the distinguished basis of $M(\lambda)$) and
$$e_t:=z_\lambda T_{d_\mu(t)}\in P(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)).$$
For row-standard $\lambda$-tableaux $u,v$ write $u\le v$ when for all
$m,k\ge1$ the first $k$ rows of $u$ contain at most as many labels $\le m$ as
the first $k$ rows of $v$, and let $t'$ be the transpose of $t$, a standard
$\lambda$-tableau. Then:

1. $\{e_t:t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is an $R$-basis of $P(\lambda)$, so
   $P(\lambda)$ is free of rank $f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$, and
   the inclusion $P(\lambda)\subseteq M(\lambda)$ splits as a map of
   $R$-modules.

2. For every $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)$ one has, with coefficients
   $a_{r,t}\in R$,
   $$e_t=q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}\,b_{t'}+\sum_{r<t'}a_{r,t}\,b_r,$$
   where the sum runs over the row-standard $r$ with $r\le t'$, $r\ne t'$; the
   square minor with rows $\{t':t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is therefore
   triangular with respect to any linear extension of the order $\le$ on
   $\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$, with diagonal entries
   $q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}$, all units of $R$.

3. The Gram matrix of the DJ form in the basis $\{e_t\}$ is
   $$B_{tu}=\sum_{r}a_{r,t}a_{r,u}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}\qquad(t,u\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)),$$
   where $a_{r,t}$ denotes the full coefficient of $b_r$ in $e_t$: it is $q^{\ell(d_\mu(t))}$ for $r=t'$, the displayed lower coefficient for $r<t'$, and zero otherwise. Unit triangularity is a property of the
   embedding, not of the Gram matrix: $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ may be degenerate.

4. Let $(i,j)$ be a Garnir node of $\mu$, that is, a node of $\mu$ with
   $j\le\mu_{i+1}$, put
   $\alpha=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_{i-1},j-1,\mu_i+1,\mu_{i+1}-j,\mu_{i+2},\dots)$
   with zero parts deleted and $D:=S_\alpha\cap D_\mu$, and let
   $\theta(T_d)\in H$ be the product of the elements
   $\theta(T_r)=(q-1)-T_r$ over a reduced word of $d$
   ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]). Then
   $$z_\lambda\sum_{d\in D}\theta(T_d)=0\qquad\text{in }P(\lambda).$$
   The coefficients are determined by the finite coset identity of step 2.2 and
   survive every base change; together with the unit minor of clause 2 these
   relations give a finite straightening of the elements $z_\lambda T_w$ to
   the standard basis $\{e_t\}$.

5. Every clause is compatible with the base change
   $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$. The proof
   uses no generic semisimplicity, divides by no quantum factorial and uses no
   choice principle.

items.title: Theta transports the Murphy cellular structure to the signed cell modules
items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$, $\lambda\vdash n$, and let
$\theta$ be the involutive automorphism of
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. Let $m_{st}$, the ideals
$I^{\unrhd\lambda}$, $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, the cell module
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, its basis classes $m_t$ and the Murphy form
$G_\lambda$ be as in
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]. Then:

1. For standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$ one has
   $\theta(m_{st})=\theta(T_{d(s)}^*)\,\theta(m_\lambda)\,\theta(T_{d(t)})$
   with $\theta(m_\lambda)=\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda$;
   the family $\{\theta(m^\mu_{st}):\mu\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$
   is again an $R$-basis of $H$; the spans $\theta(I^{\unrhd\lambda})$ and
   $\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})$ of the $\theta$-images of the corresponding basis
   elements are two-sided ideals of $H$, and the transported family is again a
   cellular basis with the same dominance poset, whose ideal filtration is the
   $\theta$-image of the original one. The image ideals are in general
   *different* subspaces from the originals: over $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, already for $n=2$ and
   $\lambda=(2)$ one has $\theta(x_{(2)})=q-T_1\notin R(1+T_1)=I^{\unrhd(2)}$.
   The poset is preserved; the ideal subspaces are not, in general.

2. The assignment $m\mapsto\theta(m)$ on representatives is a well-defined
   isomorphism of right $H$-modules
   $$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta\longrightarrow \theta(M(\lambda))/\bigl(\theta(M(\lambda))\cap\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})\bigr),$$
   whose target is the cell module of the transported basis; in particular
   $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ is free of rank $f^\lambda$ with basis
   $\{\theta(m_t):t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ and satisfies the
   transported cell law with the same coefficients.

3. The transported form $G_\lambda^\theta$, defined on the transported basis
   by $G_\lambda^\theta(\theta x,\theta y):=G_\lambda(x,y)$ for
   $x,y\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, i.e. read on the underlying module of
   $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ by $G_\lambda^\theta(x,y)=G_\lambda(x,y)$,
   is symmetric, is associative for the twisted action in the sense
   $G_\lambda^\theta(x\cdot h,y)=G_\lambda^\theta(x,y\cdot h^*)$, and has the
   same radical as $G_\lambda$; the map $x\mapsto\theta(x)$ is an isometry from
   the twisted cell module onto the cell module of the transported basis. All
   identities specialize under every base change.

4. In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is free of rank
   $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ and carries the transported form
   $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$. No choice principle is used.

## Statement

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$, $\lambda\vdash n$, and let
$\theta$ be the involutive automorphism of
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. Let $m_{st}$, the ideals
$I^{\unrhd\lambda}$, $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, the cell module
$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, its basis classes $m_t$ and the Murphy form
$G_\lambda$ be as in
[[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]. Then:

1. For standard $\lambda$-tableaux $s,t$ one has
   $\theta(m_{st})=\theta(T_{d(s)}^*)\,\theta(m_\lambda)\,\theta(T_{d(t)})$
   with $\theta(m_\lambda)=\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda$;
   the family $\{\theta(m^\mu_{st}):\mu\vdash n,\ s,t\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$
   is again an $R$-basis of $H$; the spans $\theta(I^{\unrhd\lambda})$ and
   $\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})$ of the $\theta$-images of the corresponding basis
   elements are two-sided ideals of $H$, and the transported family is again a
   cellular basis with the same dominance poset, whose ideal filtration is the
   $\theta$-image of the original one. The image ideals are in general
   *different* subspaces from the originals: over $A=\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$, already for $n=2$ and
   $\lambda=(2)$ one has $\theta(x_{(2)})=q-T_1\notin R(1+T_1)=I^{\unrhd(2)}$.
   The poset is preserved; the ideal subspaces are not, in general.

2. The assignment $m\mapsto\theta(m)$ on representatives is a well-defined
   isomorphism of right $H$-modules
   $$C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta\longrightarrow \theta(M(\lambda))/\bigl(\theta(M(\lambda))\cap\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})\bigr),$$
   whose target is the cell module of the transported basis; in particular
   $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ is free of rank $f^\lambda$ with basis
   $\{\theta(m_t):t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)\}$ and satisfies the
   transported cell law with the same coefficients.

3. The transported form $G_\lambda^\theta$, defined on the transported basis
   by $G_\lambda^\theta(\theta x,\theta y):=G_\lambda(x,y)$ for
   $x,y\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, i.e. read on the underlying module of
   $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ by $G_\lambda^\theta(x,y)=G_\lambda(x,y)$,
   is symmetric, is associative for the twisted action in the sense
   $G_\lambda^\theta(x\cdot h,y)=G_\lambda^\theta(x,y\cdot h^*)$, and has the
   same radical as $G_\lambda$; the map $x\mapsto\theta(x)$ is an isometry from
   the twisted cell module onto the cell module of the transported basis. All
   identities specialize under every base change.

4. In particular $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ is free of rank
   $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ and carries the transported form
   $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^\times$, $n\ge0$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$, the involution $\theta$ with $\theta(T_i)=(q-1)-T_i$, the Murphy basis elements $m_{st}=T_{d(s)}^*x_\lambda T_{d(t)}$, the dominance ideals $I^{\unrhd\lambda}$, $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$ and the Murphy form $G_\lambda$.

[F1] $\theta$ is an involutive $R$-algebra automorphism with $\theta(T_w)=(-q)^{\ell(w)}T_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$ that commutes with the star anti-involution $*$, satisfies $\theta(x_\rho)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\rho))}y_\rho$ for every partition $\rho$ and is base-change compatible ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).

[F2] The Murphy basis $\{m^\mu_{st}\}$ is an $R$-basis of $H$ with $m_{st}^*=m_{ts}$, the spans $I^{\unrhd\rho}$ and $I^{\rhd\rho}$ are two-sided ideals, $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)=M(\rho)/(M(\rho)\cap I^{\rhd\rho})$ is free with basis $m_t=x_\rho T_{d_\rho(t)}+I^{\rhd\rho}$, the cell law $m_{st}h\equiv\sum_v r_v m_{sv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\rho}}$ has coefficients $r_v$ independent of $s$, and the form $G_\rho$ satisfies $m_{us}m_{tv}\equiv G_\rho(m_s,m_t)m_{uv}\pmod{I^{\rhd\rho}}$, is symmetric and associative: $G_\rho(m_sh,m_t)=G_\rho(m_s,m_th^*)$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F3] Dominance is a partial order under which $I^{\rhd\rho}$ is spanned by the $m^\mu_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\rho$ ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] Base change: all formulas have coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ and specialize to any commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$ ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The $\theta$-image of the Murphy basis.** Since $\theta$ is an $R$-algebra automorphism of $H$ and $\{m^\mu_{st}\}$ is an $R$-basis by [F2], the family $\{\theta(m^\mu_{st})\}$ is again an $R$-basis, and $\theta(m_{st})=\theta(T_{d(s)}^*)\theta(x_\lambda)\theta(T_{d(t)})$ by multiplicativity, with $\theta(x_\lambda)=q^{\ell(w_0(S_\lambda))}y_\lambda$ by [F1]; also $\theta(m_{st})^*=\theta(m_{st}^*)=\theta(m_{ts})$ because $\theta$ commutes with $*$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 **The transported ideals and cellular structure.** For a partition $\rho$, the ideal $I^{\unrhd\rho}$ is spanned by the $m^\mu_{uv}$ with $\mu\unrhd\rho$ by [F3], so its image $\theta(I^{\unrhd\rho})$ is spanned by the corresponding $\theta(m^\mu_{uv})$; as the image of a two-sided ideal under an automorphism it is a two-sided ideal, and likewise for $\theta(I^{\rhd\rho})$. Moreover $\theta(I^{\unrhd\rho})\subseteq\theta(I^{\unrhd\rho'})$ whenever $\rho\unrhd\rho'$, and the transported cell law holds: for $h\in H$, $\theta(m_{st})\theta(h)=\theta(m_{st}h)\equiv\sum_v r_v\theta(m_{sv})\pmod{\theta(I^{\rhd\rho})}$ with the same coefficients $r_v$ as in [F2], independent of the first index. Hence $(\{\theta(m_{st})\},\unrhd)$ is a cellular basis with the same dominance poset and the $\theta$-image filtration. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 **The ideal subspaces move.** Take $n=2$ and $\lambda=(2)$. Here $x_{(2)}=1+T_1$ spans $I^{\unrhd(2)}=R(1+T_1)$ (the only Murphy shape dominating $(2)$ is $(2)$ itself, with a single standard tableau), while $\theta(x_{(2)})=1+\theta(T_1)=1+(q-1)-T_1=q-T_1$. A relation $q-T_1=c(1+T_1)$ with $c\in R$ would compare the coefficients of $1$ and of $T_1$ in the standard basis and force $c=q$ and $c=-1$, hence $q=-1$, which fails over the generic Laurent ring (and over any $R$ with $q\ne-1$). Conversely, at $q=-1$ one has $q-T_1=-(1+T_1)$, so these ideals coincide. Thus they differ in general, as claimed, without asserting that they differ at every parameter. By step 1.2 both are two-sided ideals with the same shape index, so the poset is preserved but the ideal subspaces are not. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 **The module isomorphism.** Put $K:=M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$, so that $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/K$ by [F2]. The assignment $m+K\mapsto\theta(m)+\theta(K)$ on representatives $m\in M(\lambda)$ is well defined and bijective, since $\theta$ is a bijection carrying $K$ onto $\theta(M(\lambda))\cap\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})$; it is $H$-linear because for $m\in M(\lambda)$ and $h\in H$ one has $\theta(m\theta(h))=\theta(m)\theta^2(h)=\theta(m)h$ using $\theta^2=\mathrm{id}$ by [F1]. Its target is by construction the quotient of the transported row by the transported higher ideal, i.e. the cell module of the transported basis of step 1.2. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ (the same underlying module with action $m\cdot h=m\theta(h)$) is isomorphic to that transported cell row, is free of rank $f^\lambda$ with basis $\{\theta(m_t)\}$ and satisfies the transported cell law. [step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra]

3.1 **The transported form.** Define $G_\lambda^\theta$ on the underlying module of $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$ by $G_\lambda^\theta(x,y):=G_\lambda(x,y)$. Symmetry is immediate from [F2], and associativity for the twisted action follows from the ordinary associativity: $G_\lambda^\theta(x\cdot h,y)=G_\lambda(x\theta(h),y)=G_\lambda(x,y\theta(h)^*)=G_\lambda(x,y\theta(h^*))=G_\lambda^\theta(x,y\cdot h^*)$, using that $\theta$ commutes with $*$ and $\theta^2=\mathrm{id}$ by [F1]. Its radical is $\{x:G_\lambda(x,y)=0\ \forall y\}=\operatorname{rad}G_\lambda$, which is a submodule for the twisted action as well. Under the identification $x\mapsto\theta(x)$ of step 2.2 the form becomes $G_\lambda^\theta(\theta u,\theta v)=G_\lambda(u,v)$ for $u,v\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$, which is exactly the Murphy form of the transported basis, because multiplying two transported basis elements gives $\theta(m_{us})\theta(m_{tv})=\theta(m_{us}m_{tv})\equiv G_\lambda(m_s,m_t)\theta(m_{uv})\pmod{\theta(I^{\rhd\lambda})}$ by [F2]; thus $G_\lambda^\theta$ is the transported form of clause 3 and $x\mapsto\theta(x)$ is an isometry. [step 2.2, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 **Base change and the conjugate clause.** Every element, ideal, quotient and form above is defined by formulas with coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ and the identities are identities of such formulas, so they specialize along any ring map $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto q$, with $q\in R^\times$, by [F4]; in particular the transported basis stays a basis and the cell law and form identities are preserved. Applying clauses 1-3 to the conjugate partition $\lambda'$, which satisfies $f^{\lambda'}=f^\lambda$ by [F2], gives clause 4. Only the presentation of $H$, the automorphism $\theta$, the Murphy cellular structure and its form are used, so no choice principle is used. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.1, F2, F4] ∎

items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with its basis $\{m_t\}$, $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the permutation form $\beta$ on $M(\lambda)$ and the DJ form on $P(\lambda)$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]. Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit $R$-bilinear pairing $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. ## Statement

Then:

1. Setting $B_\lambda(m_s,p):=\beta(x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(s)},p)$ for $s\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)$ and $p\in P(\lambda)$ defines an explicit $R$-bilinear pairing $B_\lambda\colon C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\times P(\lambda)\to R$ that is $H$-balanced, $B_\lambda(mh,p)=B_\lambda(m,ph^*)$, and whose adjoint $c\mapsto B_\lambda(c,-)$ is an isomorphism of right $H$-modules $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\to P(\lambda)^\circ$ onto the star-contragredient module of [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. No nondegeneracy of the DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ is required.

2. Equivalently, the kernel of the quotient map $M(\lambda)\to C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ is the orthogonal complement $P(\lambda)^\perp=\{a\in M(\lambda):\beta(a,p)=0\text{ for all }p\in P(\lambda)\}$, namely $M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$; the pairing matrices in the bases $\{m_s\}$ and $\{e_t\}$ have entries $B_\lambda(m_s,e_t)=q^{\ell(d_\lambda(s))}a_{d_\lambda(s),t}$ with $e_t=\sum_d a_{d,t}b_d$, and determinant a unit of $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. ## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A commutative ring $R$, $q\in R^\times$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{R,q}(S_n)$ with its standard basis, star anti-involution, the modules $M(\lambda)=x_\lambda H\supseteq P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$, the distinguished basis $\{b_r=x_\lambda T_{d_\lambda(r)}\}$ of $M(\lambda)$ and the permutation form $\beta$, the Murphy basis $\{m^\rho_{st}\}$, the dominance ideal $I^{\rhd\lambda}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)$ with basis $\{m_s\}$ and the Murphy form $G_\lambda$.

[F1] The trace $\tau\colon H\to R$, $\tau(T_w)=\delta_{w,1}$, satisfies $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ and $\tau(a^*b)=B_0(a,b)=\delta_{u,v}q^{\ell(u)}$ for standard basis elements $a=T_u$, $b=T_v$; the bilinear form $\tau(a^*b)$ has unit diagonal in the standard basis ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], Proof step 1.3).

[F2] $M(\lambda)$ is free on $\{b_r\}$, $\beta(b_r,b_v)=\delta_{r,v}q^{\ell(d_\lambda(r))}$, and $\beta$ is $H$-contravariant; $P(\lambda)$ is free on $\{e_t=z_\lambda T_{d_\lambda'(t)}\}$ and a split direct summand of $M(\lambda)$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]], [[lem-dj-bridge-permutation-form-invariance-and-restriction]], [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]).

[F3] $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)=M(\lambda)/(M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda})$, $K:=M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is the kernel of the quotient, $I^{\rhd\lambda}$ is spanned by the Murphy elements $m^\nu_{uv}$ with $\nu\rhd\lambda$, and $\{m_s\}$ is an $R$-basis of the cell module ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]]).

[F4] $x_\kappa Hy_\rho=0$ whenever $\sum_{i\le k}\kappa_i>\sum_{i\le k}\rho'_i$ for some $k\ge1$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-parabolic-double-coset-annihilation]]).

[F5] The star-contragredient $N^\circ=\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,R)$ of a right $H$-module is a right $H$-module via $(fh)(m)=f(mh^*)$; for finite free $N$ it is finite free of the same rank and $(-)^\circ$ commutes with base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]).





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The correctly scaled universal trace formula.** Work first over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using $q=v$ as the formal parameter. For $d,e\in D_\lambda$, length additivity gives $b_d=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}T_{ud}$, and [F1] gives $\tau(b_d^*b_e)=0$ when $d\ne e$, while $\tau(b_d^*b_d)=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}q^{\ell(ud)}=q^{\ell(d)}P_\lambda(q)$, where $P_\lambda(q):=\sum_{u\in S_\lambda}q^{\ell(u)}$. By bilinearity, $$\tau(a^*b)=P_\lambda(q)\,\beta(a,b)\qquad(a,b\in M_A(\lambda)).$$ The factor $P_\lambda$ is essential; it is not generally a unit and can vanish after specialization. It is nonzero in the domain $A$, since its constant coefficient is $1$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 **Orthogonality before specialization.** Put $K_A=M_A(\lambda)\cap I_A^{\rhd\lambda}$ and $p=z_\lambda h$. For a higher Murphy element $m^\nu_{uv}=T_{d_\nu(u)}^*x_\nu T_{d_\nu(v)}$ with $\nu\rhd\lambda$, its product with $p$ after star is $$ (m^\nu_{uv})^*p=T_{d_\nu(v)}^*x_\nu\bigl(T_{d_\nu(u)}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\bigr)y_{\lambda'}h=0,$$ because $x_\nu Hy_{\lambda'}=0$ by [F4]. The outer factor multiplies a zero vector; no factor is silently discarded. Expand $k\in K_A$ in the higher Murphy basis using [F3]. Then $k^*p=0$ and step 1.1 gives $P_\lambda(q)\beta(k,p)=0$. Cancel this nonzero polynomial only in the universal domain $A$, proving $\beta(K_A,P_A)=0$. The quotient and its kernel in [F3] are base-change compatible: the quotient is free on the supplied standard basis, its kernel is the split kernel of that quotient, and the independent Murphy construction identifies its specialization with $M_R(\lambda)\cap I_R^{\rhd\lambda}$. Thus tensoring the zero pairing identity gives $\beta(K_R,P_R)=0$ for every $R$ and unit $q$. No cancellation is performed in $R$, including when $P_\lambda(q)=0$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

3.1 **The descended pairing is perfect.** Define $B_\lambda(a+K_R,p)=\beta(a,p)$; step 2.1 proves this is well defined. Since the factored adjoint is an isomorphism, this is exactly $K_R=M(\lambda)\cap I^{\rhd\lambda}$. items.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $q\in R^\times$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, and write $\mu=\lambda'$, $L=\ell(w_\lambda)$ and $N=\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))$. Let $P(\lambda)=z_\lambda H$ with its DJ form $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$, the cell module $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ with its Murphy form $G_{\lambda'}$, and the sign automorphism $\theta$ be as in [[def-dj-bridge-row-column-permutation-modules-and-polytabloids]], [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]], and let $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta$ be the $\theta$-twisted cell module of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]]. Then:

1. There is a base-change compatible isomorphism of right $H$-modules $$\Phi_\lambda\colon P(\lambda)\longrightarrow C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta,\qquad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0,\quad \Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)\ \ (h\in H),$$ where $m_0$ is the class of $x_{\lambda'}$ in $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and the right side is computed with the ordinary action on $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and read in the twist; in particular $\Phi_\lambda(e_t)=m_0\theta(T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)})$ for $t\in\operatorname{Std}(\lambda')$. For a class $m\in C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and any lift $\widetilde m\in M(\lambda')$, the inverse is $\Phi_\lambda^{-1}(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$, independently of the chosen lift.

2. With $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$ the transported form of [[lem-dj-bridge-theta-transport-of-the-cellular-structure]] and $u_\lambda(q):=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{\lambda'}))-\ell(w_\lambda)}\in A^\times$, $$G_{\lambda'}^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=u_\lambda(q)\,\beta_{P(\lambda)}(x,y)\qquad(x,y\in P(\lambda)),$$ over every commutative $R$ with $q\in R^\times$. No unnamed scalar and no potentially vanishing scalar occurs: $u_\lambda$ is the explicit unit $q^{N-L}$ in the fixed normalizations of this page.

3. Consequently $\Phi_\lambda$ maps the radical of $\beta_{P(\lambda)}$ onto the radical of $G_{\lambda'}^\theta$, the induced map between the quotients is an isomorphism, with the corresponding cell-form quotients $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including the zero-quotient case. Over a field, when the quotients are nonzero they are the simple heads; when the forms are identically zero, the displayed quotients are zero and no assertion about the actual module heads is made. Over a PID with a chosen prime, the unit-scaled form identity preserves all divisibility submodules and their reductions. One also obtains $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$ with the exact position of the dual and the twist, separating same-shape duality from conjugate-sign transport. No choice principle is used.

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The integral map.** Identify $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta$ with $\theta(M(\mu))/\theta(K_\mu)$, where $K_\mu=M(\mu)\cap I^{\rhd\mu}$. By [F2], literal left multiplication by $q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}$ kills $\theta(K_\mu)$ and induces the surjection $F:C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta\to P(\lambda)$ sending the class of $x_\mu$ to $z_\lambda$. In particular $F(m)=q^{-N}x_\lambda T_{w_\lambda}\theta(\widetilde m)$ for any row-module lift, independently of that lift. Both modules are free of rank $f^\mu=f^\lambda$; finite basis preimages give a right inverse of the square matrix of $F$, so its determinant is a unit and $F$ is an isomorphism. Set $\Phi_\lambda=F^{-1}$. Its $H$-linearity with the twisted target action gives $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda h)=m_0\theta(h)$, where this expression uses the ordinary action on the underlying Murphy module. All these matrices and their inverses lie in the universal Laurent ring and specialize by [F8]. [F1, F2, F4, F8, algebra]

2.1 **Generic uniqueness of the forms, after the integral isomorphism.** Work over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with formal $q=v$ and $K=\mathbb Q(v)$. The matrix of the regular trace form $(a,b)\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_K(L_{ab})$ has Laurent-polynomial entries. At $v=1$ its matrix is $n!$ times the permutation matrix $u\leftrightarrow u^{-1}$: in the regular group basis left multiplication by a nonidentity group element has trace zero, whereas the identity has trace $n!$. Its determinant is therefore nonzero, so the regular trace form is nonsingular over $K$. If $a\in J(H_K)$, every $ab$ is nilpotent by [F6], and $L_{ab}$ has trace zero; nondegeneracy forces $a=0$, so $H_K$ is semisimple. To justify the consequence used next, any quotient algebra of a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra has semisimple regular module: the images of its finitely many simple summands are simple or zero and span the quotient; selecting successively images not contained in their predecessors expresses it as a direct sum of simples. A square-zero two-sided ideal $J$ of such an algebra acts trivially on every simple module, since $JS$ is either $0$ or $S$ and the latter would force $J^2S=S$; it therefore annihilates the semisimple regular module and is zero. Each cellular layer is an ideal in a quotient of this semisimple algebra, with multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=G_\mu(b,c)a\otimes d$. If $G_\mu$ had a nonzero radical, $(\operatorname{rad}G_\mu)\otimes C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)$ would be a nonzero square-zero ideal of that quotient, stable under its surrounding algebra by the cell law and contravariance, a contradiction. Thus $G_\mu$ is nonsingular, and the cellular rank-one operators realize the full matrix algebra on $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)_K$. Every module endomorphism is scalar because it commutes with all matrix units; this conclusion also holds on the $\theta$-twist, since $\theta(H_K)=H_K$. On that twist, any contravariant form $B'$ defines an operator $U$ by $G_\mu^\theta(Ux,y)=B'(x,y)$. Contravariance and nonsingularity imply that $U$ commutes with the module action, so $B'$ is a scalar multiple of $G_\mu^\theta$. No generic argument was used to establish the integral map or basis. [F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **The exact generator computation.** The expansion in [F2] has distinct distinguished row-module vectors and length $L+\ell(u)$, so [F3] gives $$\beta(z_\lambda,z_\lambda)=\sum_{u\in S_\mu}q^{-2\ell(u)}q^{L+\ell(u)}=q^L\sum_{u\in S_\mu}q^{-\ell(u)}=q^{L-N}P_\mu(q).$$ The last equality pairs $u$ with $w_0(S_\mu)u$. The row identity $x_\mu T_u=q^{\ell(u)}x_\mu$ gives $x_\mu^2=P_\mu(q)x_\mu$, so the defining cell product in [F4] gives $G_\mu(m_0,m_0)=P_\mu(q)$. Therefore, with the specified normalization $\Phi_\lambda(z_\lambda)=m_0$, the only possible comparison unit is $u_\lambda(q)=q^{N-L}$. This computation uses the distinguished-basis definition of $\beta$, not any incorrectly unscaled trace identity. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **Universal form identity.** Transfer the DJ form to $C_{\mathrm M}(\mu)^\theta$ using $F=\Phi_\lambda^{-1}$: set $B'(c,d)=\beta(Fc,Fd)$. This is contravariant for the twisted action, as is $G_\mu^\theta$. Both are nonzero over $K$, since their respective generator values are $q^{L-N}P_\mu(q)$ and $P_\mu(q)$, nonzero in that field. Step 2.1 makes them proportional, and step 2.2 determines the scalar as $q^{N-L}$, proving $G_\mu^\theta(\Phi_\lambda x,\Phi_\lambda y)=q^{N-L}\beta(x,y)$ over $K$. Both sides have matrices in $A$; the injection $A\to K$ proves their equality already in $A$, and then [F8] specializes it to every commutative $R$ with unit parameter. No cancellation of $P_\mu(q)$ takes place after specialization. [F3, F4, F5, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 **Radicals, divisibility, quotients and duality.** The unit form identity and the isomorphism $\Phi_\lambda$ identify the form radicals and yield $D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}}\cong(D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including zero quotients. Over a field, a vector outside a nonzero cell-form radical generates its whole cell module: choose a vector pairing to $1$ and use its finite basis expansion in the cell rank-one action $x m_{uv}=G_\mu(x,m_u)m_v$. Thus every proper submodule lies in that radical, making it the unique maximal submodule and the nonzero form quotient the simple head; transfer this conclusion through $\Phi_\lambda$. If the form is identically zero only the zero form quotient is asserted, not a zero actual head. Over a PID with chosen prime $\pi$, the submodules $\{x:\beta(x,P(\lambda))\subseteq\pi^iR\}$ for every $i\ge0$ are identified with their Murphy counterparts because the forms differ by a unit; their reductions correspond as well. Applying step 1.1 to $\lambda'$ gives $P(\lambda')\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)^\theta$. Compose with the same-shape perfect pairing [F7] and the commuting of star dual with $\theta$ in [F1] to obtain $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$. Empty shapes have $N=L=0$, $\Phi=1$ and unit $1$. This proves all clauses, using generic semisimplicity only for uniqueness of forms on an already integral module. No choice principle is used. [F1, F4, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.statement:
Assume the isomorphism $\Phi_\lambda$ and the exact unit identity of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]. Then:

1. For every commutative ring $R$ and $q=1$, the module $P(\lambda)$ identifies with the ordinary integral-polytabloid Specht module $R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ of [[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]], with the classical left action converted to a right action by $x\cdot w=w^{-1}x$: the basis $\{e_t=z_\lambda T_{d_{\lambda'}(t)}\}$ specializes to the standard polytabloid basis and the DJ form to the standard tabloid form. [F5] The Hecke algebra has presentation $(T_i-q)(T_i+1)=0$, braid and distant commutation, with standard basis $(T_w)_w$; $S_n$ has the Coxeter presentation $s_i^2=1$ with the same braid and distant commutation relations ([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], [[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]]). The row-module and polytabloid bases are split and compatible with every coefficient-ring base change ([[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]], [[lem-dj-bridge-integral-murphy-and-polytabloid-straightening]]).

[F6] The Murphy cell law and the cell form are defined by formulas with coefficients in $\mathbb Z[q^{\pm1}]$ and commute with base change; the independent same-shape perfect pairing gives $C_{\mathrm M}(\rho)\cong P(\rho)^\circ$ ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]]).





## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The group algebra over every coefficient ring.** Let $R$ be any commutative ring and specialize at $q=1$. The Hecke relations become $T_i^2=1$, braid and distant commutation. The Coxeter presentation in [F5] therefore gives the homomorphism $H_{R,1}(S_n)\to R[S_n]$ carrying $T_i$ to $s_i$. A reduced word shows that it carries every $T_w$ to $w$. These are bases of the source and target over $R$, so the map is an isomorphism over $R$, including in positive characteristic and with zero divisors. Equivalently the assignment $s_i\mapsto T_i$ gives its inverse directly from the presentation. No complex-field specialization, dimension comparison over a field or semisimplicity is used. [F5, algebra]

1.2 **Multiplicities and zero quotients.** For a field and unit $q$, the unit form identity in [F1] identifies $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ with $(D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M})^\theta$, including zero quotients. A nonzero cell-form quotient is simple: the cell rank-one action shows that every vector outside its radical generates the cell module, so the radical is its unique maximal submodule. Thus when $D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}\ne0$, the module $D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}$ is a legitimate simple composition-factor label. Applying the exact twist equivalence in [F2] to a composition series and using [F1] gives $$[P(\lambda):D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')^\theta:D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}}]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):(D^{\mu}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta]=[C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'):D^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}].$$ This proves clause 2. If a form is identically zero, only its zero form quotient is asserted; no claim is made that the actual module head vanishes. [F1, F2, F6, algebra]

2.1 **The actual polytabloids and the forms.** Give the classical tabloid module the right action $\{t\}\cdot w=\{w^{-1}\cdot t\}=\{t\cdot w\}$. The map $b_d=x_\lambda T_d\mapsto\{t^\lambda\cdot d\}$ sends the distinguished basis to the tabloid basis. It respects the right action: at $q=1$ the row-module multiplication rule is simply the permutation of these cosets, with a same-row transposition acting as $1$. Every diagonal value of $\beta$ becomes $1$, so this is an isometry to the orthonormal tabloid form. The column group of the column-filled tableau $t_\lambda$ is exactly $S_{\lambda'}$, because its columns carry the consecutive row blocks of $\lambda'$. Hence $z_\lambda=x_\lambda w_\lambda\sum_{u\in S_{\lambda'}}\operatorname{sgn}(u)u$ maps to $\sum_u\operatorname{sgn}(u)\{t_\lambda\cdot u\}$, the classical column polytabloid of $t_\lambda$ (replace $u$ by $u^{-1}$ to compare with the left-action formula). Covariance shows $e_t=z_\lambda d_{\lambda'}(t)$ maps to the polytabloid of $t_\lambda\cdot d_{\lambda'}(t)=t'$, the transpose of the standard $\lambda'$-tableau $t$. Thus the actual standard bases correspond bijectively. By the split integral classical basis in [F3] and the split Hecke basis in [F5], this identifies $P(\lambda)$ with $R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$ over every $R$, and the restricted DJ form with the restricted tabloid form. [F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **The exact position of the twist.** At $q=1$, [F2] gives $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$, hence $\theta(w)=\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$. Therefore the right module $P(\lambda)^\theta$ is the sign tensor twist. Applying the involution $\theta$ to [F1] yields $$P(\lambda)^\theta\cong C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda'),$$ without a remaining twist on the Murphy cell. Combining this with the independent same-shape pairing in [F6] gives $P(\lambda)^\theta\cong P(\lambda')^\circ$. Under step 2.1, star dual is the ordinary group contragredient dual, so this is exactly the module identity $S_F^\lambda\otimes\operatorname{sgn}\cong(S_F^{\lambda'})^*$ of [F4] after converting the published left modules to right modules. This asserts the same compatible module dictionary, not an unproved equality of separately normalized explicit maps. In characteristic $2$ the sign becomes trivial at $q=1$; conjugation remains part of the identity. [F1, F2, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **Conditional Schur dictionary and conclusion.** Under the stated separate hypothesis on a Schur corner, its images at $\lambda'$ are $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')$ and $D^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$. The untwisted Murphy identities from step 3.1 and [F1], valid for arbitrary unit $q$ by involutivity of $\theta$, identify these with $P(\lambda)^\theta$ and $(D^{\lambda}_{\mathrm{DJ}})^\theta$, including the zero quotient. This proves clause 3 without a Schur theorem as a prerequisite. The actual nonzero Schur head and the Hecke cell-form quotient are distinct notions when the corner kills the former. For the empty shape, the generators, forms, twists and all isomorphisms have value $1$. All bases, maps and scalar identities are explicit and use no choice principle. [F1, F2, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

items.statement:
**Refuted claim:** the same-shape duality $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]] may be applied without a sign twist, i.e. one may conclude $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ directly.

This is false. Over $\mathbb Q$ at $q=1$ and $n=3$ the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ is the sign module, in which $T_i$ acts by $-1$, while the ordinary polytabloid module $P((3))$ and its contragredient dual are trivial, in which $T_i$ acts by $+1$. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ without $\theta$ fails in general. The correct bridge is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]; combining it with same-shape duality gives $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$, which is a different formula. No choice principle is used.

## Statement refuted

**Refuted claim:** the same-shape duality $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda)\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]] may be applied without a sign twist, i.e. one may conclude $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ directly.

This is false. Over $\mathbb Q$ at $q=1$ and $n=3$ the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ is the sign module, in which $T_i$ acts by $-1$, while the ordinary polytabloid module $P((3))$ and its contragredient dual are trivial, in which $T_i$ acts by $+1$. Hence $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\circ$ without $\theta$ fails in general. The correct bridge is $C_{\mathrm M}(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^\theta$ of [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]; combining it with same-shape duality gives $P(\lambda')\cong P(\lambda)^{\circ,\theta}$, which is a different formula. No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field $\mathbb Q$, the specialization $q=1$ of the type-$A$ Hecke algebra $H$, the polytabloid module $P((3))=z_{(3)}H$ with its DJ form, the Murphy cell module $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ with its form, and the comparison theorem [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] together with its corollary [[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]].

[F1] At $q=1$ the specialization of $H$ is the group algebra $\mathbb Q[S_3]$ and the sign automorphism $\theta$ is the pullback along $w\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(w)w$; the partitions $(3)$ and $(1^3)$ are conjugate ([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]]).

[F2] The comparison theorem gives $P((3))\cong C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ with the exact unit $u_{(3)}=q^{\ell(w_0(S_{(1^3)}))-\ell(w_{(3)})}$ ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F3] $P((3))=x_{(3)}H$ is spanned by $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$, and $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}$ for $i=1,2$; the contragredient dual of a one-dimensional module with trivial action is trivial ([[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).

[F4] In $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ one has $f^{(1^3)}=1$, the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$ contains the elements $1+T_i$, and the cell form has value $G_{(1^3)}(m_0,m_0)=1$ ([[cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary]], [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]).



## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The ordinary module is trivial.** At $q=1$ one has $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}T_w$ and $x_{(3)}T_i=\sum_wT_wT_i=\sum_wT_{ws_i}=x_{(3)}$ for each generator, because right multiplication by $s_i$ permutes the group and every $T_{ws_i}$ is again one of the summed basis elements; with the scalar carried along this reads $x_{(3)}T_i=q\,x_{(3)}=x_{(3)}$ at $q=1$, and $P((3))=x_{(3)}H=\mathbb Q\,x_{(3)}$ is one-dimensional. Its dual is therefore also one-dimensional with trivial action. [F3, algebra]

1.2 **The cell is sign.** At $q=1$ the element $1+T_i$ lies in the higher ideal $I^{\rhd(1^3)}$, because $1+T_1=x_{(2,1)}$ belongs to that two-sided ideal and conjugation by the invertible braid word $T_1T_2$ sends $T_1$ to $T_2$, so $1+T_2$ also belongs to it; hence in the one-dimensional cell $m_0(1+T_i)=0$, that is, $m_0T_i=-m_0$. The cell form value is $1$, and the module is the sign module. [F4, algebra]

2.1 **No untwisted isomorphism.** A right $H$-module isomorphism $f\colon C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))\to P((3))^\circ$ would satisfy $f(mh)=f(m)h$ for every $h$; taking $h=T_i$ and a nonzero $m$ gives $f(-m)=f(m)$ because $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))$ has $T_i$ acting by $-1$ and $P((3))^\circ$ has $T_i$ acting by $+1$, while $f(-m)=-f(m)$ in characteristic zero, so $-f(m)=f(m)$ forces $f(m)=0$, contradicting injectivity over $\mathbb Q$. Therefore no such isomorphism exists and the untwisted claim is false. The twisted statement is consistent: on $C_{\mathrm M}((1^3))^\theta$ the generator $T_i$ acts by the ordinary action of $\theta(T_i)=-T_i$, that is by $+1$, matching $P((3))$, and the unit is $u_{(3)}=1$ by [F2]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra] ∎
